description.text: Valerian rose to the Roman throne during the turbulent Crisis of the Third Century, a period marked by rapid changes in leadership and external threats. Born around 199 CE into a senatorial family, he had a modest political career before being proclaimed emperor by the troops of the Raetian legion after the death of Aemilianus in 253 CE. He immediately appointed his son, Gallienus, as co‑emperor, a move that helped stabilize the western part of the empire while he focused on the eastern front against the Sassanid Persians.

Valerian’s reign ended in dramatic fashion when he was defeated and captured by Persian king Shapur I at the Battle of Edessa in 260 CE, becoming the first Roman emperor ever taken prisoner. While in captivity, he was subjected to harsh treatment and was forced to issue a ransom, and his death in Persian hands—whether by flaying, molten gold, or other means—remains a subject of debate among historians. During his reign he also issued harsh anti‑Christian edicts, ordering the persecution and execution of numerous Christian leaders, a policy that was reversed after his son Gallienus took the throne.

curiosities.text: Valerian was the first Roman emperor to be taken captive in battle, a humiliation that shocked the empire and led to widespread instability.
He appointed his son Gallienus as co‑emperor in 253 CE, a rare instance of a Roman emperor sharing power with his heir during the Crisis of the Third Century.

Valerian’s persecution of Christians included the execution of several prominent saints such as Pope Sixtus II, Saint Lawrence, and Saint Prudent, illustrating the severity of his anti‑Christian policies.
